newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway and Iceland squabble over fisheries.
newsitem.headline: Norway and Iceland squabble over fisheries.

text.p: Icelandic Prime Minister David Oddsson protested strongly on Tuesday against the detention of an Icelandic fishing boat by Norwegian coastguards in the North Atlantic.

"This is a serious matter. We believe things should not be handled like this between friendly nations," Oddsson told Norwegian NRK radio in an interview from Reykjavik, capital of the North Atlantic island.

He demanded an explanation of the incident last Friday in which the Icelandic fishing boat Sigurdur was detained on suspicion of catching 400 tonnes of herring illegally in the zone off Norway's Jan Mayen island.
Norway sought to play down the incident, saying it had nothing to do with foreign policy but was purely a matter of upholding fishing regulations.
"We are not interested in contributing to this becoming an infected issue in our relations with Iceland," Foreign Ministry spokesman Ingvard Havnen told Reuters.
"We must keep in mind that this a matter of regulating fishing around the Jan Mayen zone."
He said the Icelandic embassy submitted a formal protest to the Norwegian Foreign Ministry on Saturday.
"We will come back with an answer to Iceland through the normal diplomatic procedures soon," Havnen said.
Norway and Iceland have had several bitter disputes over fishing quotas and rights in the Barents Sea and the North Atlantic over the past few years.
"We believe this does not bode well for the understanding of Icelandic interests in Norway," Oddsson said.

The Sigurdur was towed at the weekend to the northern Norwegian town of Bodoe, where police fined the captain, Kristbjoern Arnasaan, 30,000 Norwegian crowns ($4,190) for violating Norwegian economic zone regulations and rules for fishing herring.
The boat's owner, fishing company Isfelag, was fined 375,000 crowns on the same grounds.
The Icelanders refused to pay and the matter will come up in a Bodoe court on September 2, police said.
The dispute centres on whether or not the Sigurdur, which has a license to fish off Jan Mayen, told Norwegian fisheries authorities about its intention to fish there.

The Norwegian coast guard service says the boat made no such announcement, failing to comply with the rules, but Iceland says it has verified that the ship radioed Norwegian authorities in line with regulations.
